strengths: Addresses an important question: whether optimization methods that improve generalization can also increase membership privacy risks.

The experiments cover four image and tabular datasets, several attack families, and additional image architectures. The repeated increase in SAM’s strongest tested single-query attack accuracy is a useful empirical observation.
The influence-based stratification examines generalization beyond aggregate accuracy, with illustrative examples connecting atypical test images to influential training examples.

SharpReg is a simple objective modification with substantial reported attack reductions. On CIFAR-100, single-query attack accuracy decreases from 76.68% to 59.64%, while test accuracy decreases from 79.92% to 75.86%.
weaknesses: The central memorization explanation remains insufficiently established. The analysis uses precomputed SGD influence scores on CIFAR-100, without directly measuring how SAM changes memorization. Better performance on these buckets could reflect improved representations or example difficulty. Near-perfect accuracy in the highest buckets also creates a ceiling effect. Direct influence comparisons or controlled training-example removal experiments are needed.

The proposed entropy metric has an unresolved definition issue. Its normalization is undefined when every influence score is zero, yet Appendix C.1 assigns these cases—2,153 test images—to the highest-entropy bucket. This convention and the manually selected bucket thresholds need justification and sensitivity analysis before the metric supports a memorization spectrum.

The broad privacy claims exceed the evidence. Table 1 shows SAM reducing multi-query attack accuracy on CIFAR-100 from 69.18% to 65.41% and on CIFAR-10 from 56.36% to 54.01%. Purchase-100’s single-query increase is only 0.29 percentage points relative to the reported variability. These results require an explanation of the dependence on attack type and a narrower conclusion.

Attack reporting needs reconciliation. Equation (8) defines a correctness-only attack; under balanced membership evaluation, Table 4’s CIFAR-100 SGD accuracies imply approximately 59.84% attack accuracy, whereas Table 3 reports 77.04%. Membership priors, evaluation-subset accuracies, and the implemented attack must be specified to explain this discrepancy.

SharpReg’s claimed separate anti-overfitting mechanism is not demonstrated. For ξ < 1, Equation (5) equals (1−ξ) times Equation (4) with λ replaced by λ/(1−ξ). Thus, ξ introduces no independent objective component. Although the appendix acknowledges parameter reduction, matched sharpness-weight and optimization-scale ablations are missing.

The defense comparisons do not establish a compelling advantage. SELENA achieves both higher test accuracy and lower attack accuracy than the selected SharpReg configurations on CIFAR-100 and Texas-100 in Table 4. Comparisons against SGD with appropriately tuned early stopping and regularization, fuller tradeoff curves, and measured computational costs are needed.

Privacy evaluation remains incomplete for the stated scope: it lacks strong per-example calibrated attacks and true-positive rates at low false-positive rates. The five repetitions are described as varying attack-data splits, leaving uncertainty across independently trained victim models unclear. These limitations weaken claims of exhaustive evaluation and reliable privacy improvement.
